author: ACG
title: Labour and the budget: same old same old (with a side of pickles)
content:
When Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey presented his budget on Wednesday October 28

th

 he said: “This is a Budget for the working people of Britain. For British businesses, big and small.”  Well, no. It offered little to working people, and plenty to businesses, to the military and to the defence industry.




We were offered the pittance of 86p a week off of electricity bills. In addition, there will be a £100 one-off winter fuel payment for 20 million households in council tax bands A to D. This will almost immediately be wiped out by a predicted rise by £276 in January, to just under £2,000 a year. Another forecast from the EDF energy company, predicted that it might rise higher than this.




Healey introduced a £2 cap on single bus fares in England from January 2027. But, for example, many workers and students in London cannot afford to live in inner London and must make long journeys by bus to get to work and study, because they cannot afford the rail and tube fares.




He also announced the end of gas standing charges, which will save a mere £45 a year, and then only for 60% of households. Healey had already announced that an extra £432 million would be spent on a programme to get rough sleepers in England off the streets. Unpaid carers would no longer lose all of their Carer’s Allowance if they earnt more than 1p over the £204 allowed and instead there would be a tapered payment.




On the other hand, Healey reassured the boss class by stating that he was committed to “prevent regulation from holding back investment by removing regulation and tariffs worth £800m to business.” The banks feared that the corporation tax surcharge would be raised by as much as 8 per cent. In fact, Healey only raised it by six per cent, and smarmed the banks by saying,” I celebrate and am grateful for the role you play”. In fact, this surcharge will only last for 15 months from January. As a result, share prices of the main UK banks increased, after the budget announcement.




The Financial Times, the bosses’ voice, enthusiastically noted that Healey and Burnham wanted to reassure business and the banks.




He promised an increase of £10 billion on economic and military support for Ukraine, in addition to the £25 billion already committed by previous Tory and Labour administrations. He would also make cuts in the budgets of various government departments by 1%to further fund defence spending. As a result, the Warm Homes Plan, would suffer a £1 billion cut. He promised a maximum amount of private investment in defence, including through public private partnerships.




Labour had promised to end discriminatory age bands and to increase the minimum wage for 18- to 20-year-olds to be the same as those over 21 years old. Healey broke this promise with the 18 to 20 years olds earning nearly £2 an hour less. scrapping “discriminatory” age bands, and to increasing the minimum wages for 18- to 20-year-olds so young workers are paid the same as those over 21. Healey broke this promise—18- to 20-year-olds will still earn nearly £2 an hour less. The rate for both age levels will rise by 3.9% but this will be cancelled out by rising inflation.




Labour will use these young workers as a cheap labour force, and is already pushing an unpaid work experience scheme at Sainsbury’s.




Labour is preparing for further attacks on welfare, and Healey promised, “As the Prime Minister and I have both said, we will bring down the welfare bill.” They are eying up attacking the Personal Independence Payment, the major disability benefit. All of this is in the pipeline.




Healey did not remove the Triple Lock on pensions, and this will not happen before the 2030 election, but made the menacing statement that Labour would adjust the Triple Lock after that.




All in all, the budget was low key, with a series of minor announcements. In addition to the above, there was the removal of import tax on some 100 products, meaning cheaper prices for things like, baked beans, gherkins, garlic and marmalade. This was derided widely in the media, as this would save around £21 a year, or £1.75 a month! Parental pay would be extended, so that 150,000 parents will receive two weeks of support of up to £194 a week. Again, this will be wiped out by rising inflation.




So, no real challenge to big business and a massive increase in defence spending, with looming attacks on pensioners, young workers and the disabled. But we never expected anything else from the Burnham administration.




When Burnham assumed the leadership of the Labour Party, earlier this year, he promised to “end 40 years of neoliberalism.” This budget underlines that he, Healey and the rest of the Labour leaders remain committed to fiscal policies, which are exactly what neoliberalism requires in order to function. Nothing then has changed, with lilliputian tinkering instead of the radical change that Burnham promised.

title: SOLIDARITY WITH ALL ANTI-WAR PRISONERS IN RUSSIA & DRAFT DODGERS IN UKRAINE
content:
Beneath is the text of the leaflet distributed outside both the Russian and Ukrainian embassies in London by members of the Anarchist Communist Group and the Network of Anarchist Internationalists (NAI) on Saturday October 31st







For the past five years, the warring states of Ukraine and Russia have been sending the working class to die on the battlefields, killing civilians across the war zone and destroying critical infrastructure with missiles and drones. European states are arming Ukraine, helping to keep the war of the trenches going on indefinitely—a war that has already lasted longer than WWI—in order to lay the groundwork for the revitalisation of their declining industry by shifting it more and more toward a war economy. The endless war, financed by loans from Europe and the USA, allows states to carry out their ideological, bureaucratic and technical “defensive” restructuring, as well as the broader restructuring of production, at a time when the US is pulling back from funding the war in the region and the whole planet is beginning to smell of gunpowder. The loans under the Rearm Europe arms program and the record ‘defence’ budgets being pushed by Europe point with certainty toward war austerity, in other words an even harsher exploitation of the working class, as its future wages are put up as collateral for current spending. In 2025, global military spending reached $2.887 trillion, the highest level ever recorded by SIPRI, while Europe increased its military spending by 14% in a single year. European military spending reached an average of 3.2% of GDP, up from 2.8% in 2024.




The Death Camp that is Ukraine, hemmed in on all sides, built jointly by Russia on the one hand and the USA and Europe on the other, plays a key role in spreading militarisation throughout European societies: expanding the arms industry, increasing military spending, intensifying and generalising conscription, recruiting men and, to

some extent, women into the armed forces with the lure of a career, and repressing those who refuse to take part.




Within this process, desertion and draft resistance movements play an important role in undermining the ideology of national unity and the state’s ability to keep mobilising entire populations for war. This is why the widespread draft resistance and desertion in Ukraine and Russia—300,000 deserters and 2,000,000 draft dodgers in the former, and more than 75,000 deserters and 260,000 draft dodgers as early as September 2022 in the latter—is so significant and deserves the support of the antiwar movement. The stories of violence and imprisonment suffered by those resisting mobilization on both sides of the front show what the militarisation of society means

in practice, and what it costs to refuse to fight for the state and the bosses.




In Russia, which has recently entered a phase of silent mass mobilisation, deserters—most of them forcibly recruited through coercion and blackmail—are being summarily executed on the spot by their own commanders (zeroing out). Along the borders of Ukraine, men trapped inside the country by martial law—which prevents them from leaving for safer countries—are trying to cross frozen mountains and rivers to escape

mobilisation. Some freeze to death; others drown. Those forced to remain in the country are left at the mercy of the TRCs, a special military unit that rounds up men from the streets, their workplaces, public transport stops, cafés and outside schools. They are thrown into vans and taken to the front in a practice that has become known

as busification’. Those who physically resist busification or take part in armed resistance inside training centers end up facing crushing prison sentences. When an army lifer is killed in such an incident, the sentence is life imprisonment.




Bogdan Koshel, 27, was drafted in Kyiv in June 2025. After contemplating suicide, he eventually turned his weapon on the military bastards who were training him and was sentenced to life in prison on June 9, 2026, for the deaths of two of them. Twenty three-year-old Oleg Gavrilov and five others arrested under martial law for

“obstructing mobilization” during the July 8, 2026 uprising in a neighborhood of Lviv against a busification operation are being prosecuted for assault against police officers. Twenty-seven-year-old Ukrainian Trotskyist Bogdan Syrotiuk was sentenced to 15 years in prison not for any physical attack or act of resistance, but simply for expressing antiwar views in articles published on the World Socialist Website. These are only a few of the hundreds who have disappeared into state cells, with no solidarity network to support them. Even legal defense by independent lawyers has become difficult, since they risk being subjected to busification the moment they

appear in court, or becoming targets of beatings.




Women who defend men against busification and run social-media groups documenting TRC checkpoints are also targeted by uniformed thugs, cops and far right paramilitaries. Those who support men trying to escape busification are beaten by cops, pepper-sprayed and otherwise assaulted; after their arrest, they can receive

five-year suspended sentences and be placed under supervision. Angela Gurena was sentenced to five years in prison without suspension for posting a TikTok video showing soldiers rounding up men during a busification operation.




Even civilians are thrown into so-called “penal colonies,” a soviet holdover in the prison system, because they are accused of alleged—and perhaps, in some cases, actual— “collaborationism” with the Russian administration in the formerly occupied territories. At “Penal Colony” No. 86 in Vinnytsia, alleged “collaborators” went on hunger strike on August 5 and again on September 11, protesting the brutal conditions of their detention, including torture and 12-hour forced labor.




Across Ukraine, 620 incidents of armed and/or unarmed resistance to busification and 272 attacks on TRCs have been recorded since the beginning of 2026.




On the other side of the front, in Russia, more than 20,000 people have been arrested for antiwar actions since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Some were arrested for antiwar graffiti, others for setting fire to military recruitment offices, and others for sabotaging railway lines carrying military

supplies to the front. More than 40 people had already been sentenced by the end of Russian proletarians who hit military recruitment offices with Molotov cocktails or sabotage railway lines are not always motivated exclusively by anti-militarist or antiwar convictions. In many cases they are anti-regime or motivated by pro-Ukrainian sentiments. However, even when such actions are done out of solidarity with the Ukrainian population, from pacifist or internationalist anarchist or communist convictions, they are still prosecuted as terrorism or as collaboration ‘with the enemy’.




In any case, those involved face heavy sentences and vindictive treatment inside the prisons where they are held.




The case of the ‘Chita anarchists’ is a telling example. Aleksandr Snezhkov and Lyubov Lizunova, two young people who wrote an antiwar slogan and set up an antiwar group on Telegram, were convicted as terrorists. Aleksandr was sentenced to 11 years in prison, while 17-year-old Lyubov was sent to a juvenile penal colony far from where herfamily lives. The anarchist Alexey Rozhkov was sentenced to 16 years in prison for throwing a Molotov cocktail at a military recruitment office, which, much to our regret,

caused minor damage.




Some men in Russia who took a stand against the war have lost their lives. Among them was 43-year-old anarchist pacifist Dmitry Kuznetsov, who died after being beaten and tortured in prison, and 20-year-old conscript Seryozha Gridin, who died by suicide in February 2023 at a military base near Moscow rather than fight in Ukraine. In a note, he wrote: “I decided to die here, in my homeland, without foreign blood on

my hands.”




Imprisoned Russian activists are calling for contact with the internationalist antiwar movement. Through their relatives and lawyers, they have made clear that they can endure prison, but not isolation. Contact addresses for reaching them are available through Solidarity Zone and the Anarchist Black Cross.

https://solidarityzone.net/political-prisoners/

https://wiki.avtonom.org/en/index.php/Category:Currently_imprisoned_in_Russia

WE STAND WITH DESERTERS AND DRAFT EVADERS

IMPRISONED ENEMIES OF WAR, YOU ARE NOT ALONE

title: From France to Portugal to Spain and Around the World: Uprisings and State Violence
content:
“If high school and university students are accused of violence today, it is merely a smokescreen. The real violence, the only violence, is still and always on the side of governments, capitalist policies, and the State that wants to save money at the expense of our lives and the future of our youth.

They are rising up for better living and educational conditions. They are rising up for all of us. They are rising up for their parents. They are rising up for those who work and are exploited. It rises up against the true and only violence that exists: that of the authorities announcing a new austerity program of 54 billion euros, cuts to public services, education, hospitals, and social security.”




From a statement of the Fédération Anarchiste of France.




“The government, overwhelmed, no longer knows what tactic to use to divide the current social movement, between the “good ” peaceful protesters and the “bad” vandals and looters. We reject this division and advocate for a diversity of tactics; our solidarity goes to the victims of repression and state violence. While a protester has died in Paris, we strongly reject the indecent injunction to  “condemn the violence” of the social movement. The society of precarity, racism, and war that the government has forged with the bourgeoisie can only sow misery and generate anger. Widespread social inequalities lead to the direct socialization of goods that are becoming increasingly inaccessible. We will only have what we take.”   




From a statement from the Union Communiste Libertaire.




In France, in Belgium, in Portugal and Spain, in Italy, in Greece, in Albania and Argentina, we have seen mass mobilisations, confrontations with the police attack dogs, blockades of roads and ports, strikes and State buildings attacked. This reflects a growing anger throughout the working class internationally against austerity programmes, rising food and energy prices, rising rents and lack of housing and worsening conditions.




Alongside this is disquiet about the worsening climate crisis, increasing State control, surveillance and repression, and the drive to war.




In 

France

 on October 17

th

, 1 million people mobilised against the rising cost of living. There were included 100,000 in Bordeaux, 80,000 in Toulouse, 60,000 in Nantes, 60,000 in Lille, 50,000 in Lyon, 40,000 in Montpellier, 30,000 in Strasbourg, 30,000 in Grenoble, 20,000 in Rennes, and 20,000 in Rouen. There were vast numbers in Paris, Marseille, and other cities where the police attacked demonstrations very early.  In Marseille, students, workers and supporters of the Yellow Vests set up barricades. City Hall and a police station   were attacked, as well as several large chain stores.

There were attacks on government buildings and blockades of highways and train stations. The police response was vicious. One paramedic died in Paris after being beaten by the cops. A 17-year-old girl lost her eye after being hit by a tear gas canister, and hundreds of others have been injured with more than 2,400 arrests.




This is in the context of the ongoing movement of high school students, now joined by university students. The uprising in France appears to have acted as a spark to ignite social conflagrations in other countries.




In 

Italy

, on the 16

th

 October, more than 400,000 students took to the streets in over 40 Italian cities for the “No Meloni Day” protests, demonstrating against the high cost of living and the racist and militaristic policies of Giorgia Meloni’s right-wing government. In Rome, students targeted the Ministry of Education building, which was heavily guarded by riot police. In Bologna, clashes with the police broke out in front of the city’s central train station. In Turin, clashes with police occurred when students attempted to approach the Prefecture.




Across the country, dozens of schools and universities have been occupied by students, who reported intimidation by police forces—including nighttime searches of their homes, arrests, and requirements to report regularly to police stations. A general strike was called for the following day, with a national demonstration in Rome.




Thousands took to the streets on the 17

th

 against austerity measures, in particular the cutting of education funding in favour of military spending, and against the rising cost of livings. There were clashes with the police in Milan, Turin, Bolognia and Brescia. There were many arrests.




Another general strike has been scheduled for October 30 by grassroots unions and various social organisations.




In 

Portugal

, inspired by France and by the massive movement in Spain over the housing crisis, protest camps were set up in the city of Porto, in response to the government’s new policies that favour landlords and make evictions easier. From the start, these encampments have been under police attack. Many have been injured by the cops. In Lisbon and other cities, thousands came out on the streets. In Lisbon, the group “Não dá mais para viver assim” (We can’t go on living like this) headed up a demonstration of thousands against the rising cost of living, unaffordable housing and wages not able to even fulfil basic needs. There was a similar demonstration in Coimbra.




For many young people “working hard” is no longer enough to secure a decent home. On average, Portuguese people can only afford to leave their parents’ home at age 29. Portugal’s national minimum wage has been reported at around €820 a month after tax, while renting a one-bedroom flat in Porto can cost up to €1,215 a month. Rents have risen by more than 100 percent over the past decade.




In 

Belgium,

 protests by high school students began on October 1

st

, ignited by the French events. Demonstrations in Brussels and Liege against cuts in education funding and budget cuts began, with police repeatedly attacking with water cannon and tear gas canisters. There were many arrests, and barricades were thrown up to protect against the police attacks.




In Liege, the motorway was blockaded, and again barricades were built.  




Belgian Interior Minister Bernard Quintin said in a post on X/Twitter that “what is unfolding in Brussels is no longer mere protest” and “all necessary means will be used to restore order in the face of the rioters.” The government moved to ban demonstrations.




Further afield, in Colombia, in South America, a major strike began on the 14

th

 October against the neoliberal policies of President Abelardo de la Espriella. Tens of thousands of people took to the streets in Colombia’s major cities to protest against a new decree that criminalises social protest, and to demand improvements to working conditions and the education system. The mobilizations come one day after the entry into force of Decree 1525, which “defines the new protocol for how authorities should act during public demonstrations” and legitimises the use of force by the police at such events.




There were attacks by the police on demonstrations in Medellin, Cali, Ibagué and Bucaramanga. In Popayán, protesters attacked the offices of the governor and the mayor. Police used tear gas to disperse the demonstrators.




In 

Mexico

, the police attacked a demonstration over contaminated drinking water that had flooded many homes on 12

th

 October. When the demonstration arrived at the official residence of the governor of Jalisco state, in Guadalajara, they were attacked by cops, who arrested 39 people.




In 

Chile

, on 12

th

 October, on the National Day of Resistance of the Peoples, various indigenous and social organisations took to the streets to demand protection, autonomy, and an end to the militarization of indigenous territories, as well as the release of Mapuche political prisoners.




Riot police repeatedly used tear gas in an attempt to split the march in two and arrested 17 people.




Not Just the Youth




It should be remembered that it is not just youth, and in particular high school students, involved in mobilisations. In France there was a national mobilisation in support of the public services that was initiated by the firefighters. The high school students threw their support behind this. In addition, university students have also come out in support of the demands of the high school students. Education workers and other workers have also given their support to the mobilisations, in some instances going out on strike in support.




Whose Violence?




At least 170 students have been seriously injured by the cops. One student lost the use of his right eye; one paramedic died in Paris after being beaten by the cops. A 17-year-old girl lost her eye after being hit by a tear gas canister. Another lost his teeth and suffered a double fracture to the jaw after being hit by a rubber bullet. One cop arrested a high school student and held his head under water. Many were throttled, some into unconsciousness. One student lost a hand, another an arm. Demonstrations were consistently targeted by the cops, who used violent measures like tear gas, pepper sprays, rubber bullets, water cannon and baton charges. The violence we see comes from the State, whilst anyone who fights back against this is seen as a violent thug.




Despite this brutality, the movement grows. The deployment of 70,000 tooled up cops failed to deter the massive demonstrations on October 24

th

. Hundreds of thousands in Paris, tens of thousands of people in Marseille, 20,000 in Lyon, 10,000 in Bordeaux, and at least 30,000 people in Orléans.




This movement in Europe and further afield, is the biggest since 1968. However, as yet workers have not come out in significant strikes and occupations as happened then. The developing movement must link up to the dockers’ international actions against war and militarism on October 30

th

. The decision by the different trade union centrals in France to call a one-day general strike on November 5

th

 must lead to workers attempting to extend strike action beyond just one day to an indefinite general strike and to workplace occupations. The union bureaucrats are calling the November 5

th

 strike to try and tame the movement. They have consistently acted against unity between students and workers, marching union contingents off separately from those of the students on demonstrations.




President Macron of France, has condemned “unbridled” violence, not that of his vicious police thugs, but the defensive actions of demonstrators, and blamed hooligans, criminals and the “ultra-left”. It is hardly surprising that the far-right National Rally, led by Marine Le Pen, endorsed this. Andy Burnham’s government has stated that the violence in France is “unacceptable”, not referring to the State violence. Burnham and co. are worried that the unrest in continental Europe will spread to the UK.




If that happened, the Burnham regime would use exactly the same tactics used by governments in the rest of Europe.

title: CITIZENSHIP LAWS IN IRELAND
content:
The coalition government in the south of Ireland is proposing to change the rules surrounding citizenship. At the moment it takes 5 years to become a naturalised citizen. The intention of Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration James O’Callaghan, is that it will require 8 years. In addition, you can’t have had welfare payments in the last 2 years of that period. Plus you need to show you have a certain level of ability in Irish or English. Let’s look at what is driving these revisions.




The change seems to come out of nowhere. One of  O’Callaghan’s explicitly declared reasons for the modification of the law is a technical one. He says that Ireland is an outlier in European Union (EU) terms and should be brought into line with EU norms. He cited Germany as an example of a country that requires an 8 year wait. The trouble is, this is just factually not true. Germany actually reduced its requirements from 8 to 5 years in 2024 (https://www.bmi.bund.de/SharedDocs/kurzmeldungen/EN/2024/06/mod-staatsangehoerigkeitsrecht.html).




 In reality, there are a variety of conditions across the EU. Twelve of the 27 member states have a standard residence requirement of five years for naturalisation, according to a report published in 2025 by the Robert Schuman Centre for Advanced Studies (https://globalcit.eu/new-globalcit-study-compares-conditions-for-citizenship-acquisition-by-

author: Erica Malatesta
title: Scotland: Anti-Data Centre Movement Gathers Momentum
content:
“Every time you ask ChatGPT a question, read a Google summary or make an online bank payment, a data centre is working behind the scenes. Now Scotland is part of a global race to build many more of them – on a massive scale. The explosion in artificial intelligence (AI) over the past few years has seen tech firms scrambling to build new “hyperscale” data centres, including some which would rank among the biggest in the world. Plans are in place to build at least 23 giant AI-powered data centres” (

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6qxv55882z1o

).




AI has insinuated itself into all areas of life and society. For example in education, it has managed to secure huge contracts with universities and schools, leading to the forcing of AI on teachers and students.




AI is controlled by Big Tech capitalists and by heads of state. It hopes to create huge dividends for shareholders and profits for its owners while claiming to be good for society.




AI has not stopped war. It is developing techniques to destroy cities and kill people remotely. title: REBELLION IN ALBANIA
content:
On October 15, the third day of the uprising and after 138 days of peaceful daily demonstrations, the streets of Tirana were under the control of students. A small student demonstration joined the protest, demanding better educational conditions. The brutal police violence against this group turned out to be the last straw – it prompted first the students, then the rest of the population, and now high school students to speak out against police brutality and demand the resignation of the Prime Minister, the government, and the complete dismantling of their entire system.




Protesters demanding the fall of the government engaged in fierce clashes with the police. Thousands of students boycotted classes and took to the streets alongside thousands of citizens from the “Flamingo Revolution” movement to protest against a corrupt system and its primary representative, the country’s Prime Minister, Edi Rama, and demanding the latter’s resignation. He has given protected natural areas to Trump’s daughter and son-in-law, Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner, for the construction of a luxury hotel complex.




During the clashes, which lasted late into the night, the buildings housing the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Economy and Finance, the Ministry of Justice, and the Constitutional Court—as well as a police station and several bank branches—were attacked and set on fire.

title: NON-VIOLENCE DOES NOT EXIST
content:
The text below appeared in the  journal of the Organisation Communiste Libertaire (OCL) of France, Courant Alternatif. Whilst specific French instances are referred to, we feel that this is a useful general article on the question of “non-violence.”




For ages, the debate between non-violence and violence has permeated social movements. Violence is not only physical, but also institutional, symbolic, psychological, and so on. This opposition is largely fuelled by the state. It criminalises our mobilisations by accusing them of being violent, even going so far as to accuse them of terrorism or of glorifying it. It is imperative to move beyond this opposition and try to act by taking into account and articulating the multiple forms, actions, and initiatives that social movements take.




The primary function of the state is to maintain social order: capitalist society. It is founded on exploitation, the maintenance of a social hierarchy, patriarchy, and the division of the dominated among themselves, through racialisation, the subjugation of certain genders, criminalisation, and the creation of artificial competition. All of this generates daily violent conflict. Faced with challenges to these various aspects, the state has no choice but to respond violently. In this context, the debate between non-violence and violence is sterile. It only serves to perpetuate divisions within
